questions.prompt: Which layer parses and checks SQL and selects a query plan?
options: Query planning
Buffer management
Files/index management
Disk-space management
questions.explanation: Planning interprets the query and chooses a plan. The disk layer provides page storage.

questions.prompt: What does operator execution do?
options: It selects a buffer-pool victim
It runs the operators’ dataflow over records and files
It parses SQL and chooses logical rewrites
It maps page IDs to file offsets
questions.explanation: Execution carries out the plan. Page allocation belongs to a lower layer.

questions.prompt: Which abstraction does the files/index layer work with directly?
options: Only query text and syntax trees
Only frame metadata, without knowledge of records
Records organised into pages within logical files
Device sectors and head positions, bypassing pages
questions.explanation: This layer organises records and files. Lower layers hide the device’s byte-level details.

questions.prompt: What is the main distinction between the buffer manager and the disk-space manager?
options: The buffer manager chooses join order; the disk-space manager computes aggregates
The buffer manager stores schemas; the disk-space manager stores only query results
The buffer manager manages record fields; the disk-space manager chooses projections
The buffer manager manages pages in RAM; the disk-space manager maps and reads/writes storage
questions.explanation: Both deal with pages, but they have different memory-management and storage responsibilities.

questions.prompt: How does the architecture diagram represent concurrency control and recovery?
options: As functions spanning several layers
As two physical join algorithms
As two fixed-length record layouts
As two types of leaf index entries
questions.explanation: They coordinate multiple parts of the system, rather than acting as individual query-result operators.

questions.prompt: Where is data normally processed in a disk-oriented DBMS?
options: Only in the query planner before any data page is read
In main memory after the required pages are read
By directly modifying sectors without loading pages into memory
Only on the persistent disk copy, without a buffer pool
questions.explanation: Data is brought into RAM for processing, although its main persistent copy may reside on disk.

questions.prompt: What does volatile memory lose when power is removed and no other preservation mechanism is available?
options: Only pages with pinCount=0
All copies on nonvolatile storage are also lost
The contents held in that memory
Only pages marked dirty=false
questions.explanation: Volatility describes the device’s own contents. It does not mean that every persistent copy is also lost.

questions.prompt: What is the general trend moving from CPU cache down to HDD in the hierarchy?
options: Faster access but smaller capacity
Every layer has identical latency
Every layer supports byte access in the same way
Slower access but larger capacity
questions.explanation: The hierarchy trades latency against capacity. Its storage layers do not all provide the same addressing capabilities.

questions.prompt: What unit does a disk-oriented read API typically transfer?
options: A page or block
Always one individual SQL field
Always the entire database
Always one character
questions.explanation: A page is the I/O abstraction. Needing one field does not imply reading only a few bytes from disk.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecture not assume that every database fits entirely in RAM?
options: Disk access is always faster than DRAM
Cost, capacity, and volatility impose constraints
The relational model forbids tuples in RAM
No main-memory system can support persistence
questions.explanation: These are system trade-offs, not restrictions imposed by SQL.

questions.prompt: What are the three components of HDD read cost in the lecture’s model?
options: Transfer time, pin count, and dirty flag
Rotational delay, query parsing, and duplicate elimination
Seek time, rotational delay, and transfer time
Seek time, buffer hit rate, and GROUP BY time
questions.explanation: These are the HDD’s mechanical and transfer costs. Buffer metadata belongs to a different concept.

questions.prompt: What does seek time measure?
options: Waiting for the required sector to rotate under the head
Transferring a block’s bytes after positioning
Finding the RAM frame holding a PageId
Moving the head to the required track
questions.explanation: Seeking moves the arm or head. Rotational delay waits for the disk to turn.

questions.prompt: An HDD runs at 12000 rpm. Assuming a uniformly distributed rotational position, what is the average rotational delay?
options: 2.5 ms
5 ms
12 ms
0.5 ms
questions.explanation: One revolution takes 60/12000 seconds=5 ms. The average wait is half a revolution, or 2.5 ms.

questions.prompt: With seek=4 ms, rotation=3 ms, and transfer=0.2 ms, what is one random read’s cost in the additive model?
options: 7 ms
7.2 ms
0.2 ms
questions.explanation: Add all three components. Counting only transfer would omit the substantial positioning cost.

questions.prompt: If only the transfer rate doubles while seek and rotation stay unchanged, must total read latency halve?
options: Yes; seek time automatically halves too
Yes; rotational delay disappears entirely
No
Yes; all read time is transfer time
questions.explanation: Only the transfer component decreases. The fixed positioning costs remain, so the total generally does not halve.

topics.title: SEQUENTIAL VS. RANDOM ACCESS / ARRANGING BLOCKS

questions.prompt: Each random read costs 6 ms for positioning and 0.1 ms for transfer. How long do 100 independent reads take when executed sequentially?
options: 16 ms
10 ms
610 ms
questions.explanation: Each read costs 6.1 ms, multiplied by 100. Independent random positions do not share a single initial positioning cost.

questions.prompt: With the same parameters, how long does one contiguous run of 100 pages take, ignoring track changes?
options: 16 ms
610 ms
6.1 ms
100 ms
questions.explanation: The run pays 6 ms initially and then 100×0.1 ms for transfer. This differs from 100 random reads.

questions.prompt: Why can prefetching a run of pages help?
options: It guarantees every future request will be a buffer hit
It spreads positioning overhead across pages and prepares data early
It automatically reduces the number of logical result records
It makes every page read transfer exactly one field
questions.explanation: Prefetch exploits locality and possible overlap. It does not change query semantics or the record layout.

questions.prompt: How should pages frequently read together be placed under the lecture’s HDD model?
options: Anywhere, because random and sequential HDD access always cost the same
Sharing a logical filename is sufficient regardless of physical placement
Close together physically
Far apart to increase the number of independent seeks
questions.explanation: Physical locality can reduce seeking and rotational costs. Sharing a primary key does not determine physical placement.

questions.prompt: Is a random/sequential comparison from one slide configuration a benchmark for every current SSD?
options: Yes; the ratio is independent of controller and workload
Yes; equal page counts guarantee equal latency
Yes; caching and parallelism do not affect the comparison
No; it is a model or example under stated assumptions
questions.explanation: Hardware and workloads differ. Slide figures do not replace measurements of the actual system.

questions.prompt: Why can small writes cause write amplification on NAND flash?
options: The erase unit is larger than the amount the application changes
Flash has a longer rotational delay than HDDs
Read pages and erase blocks always have identical granularity
Every logical write must rewrite the entire database
questions.explanation: Flash has erase/program granularities and may need to relocate data. It has no HDD-style rotating mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of wear levelling?
options: To increase each cell’s physical erase limit through SQL
To distribute writes and erases and avoid concentrated wear
To put all hot writes in one cell to reduce metadata
To sort records by search key
questions.explanation: Wear levelling manages device endurance. It is not an SQL grouping policy.

questions.prompt: Which cautious statement about SSD locality is consistent with the lecture?
options: Random writes always cost the same as sequential writes at every size
SSDs eliminate every data-layout trade-off
Random and sequential access can still have different costs
Every SSD I/O costs the same
questions.explanation: Having no moving head does not eliminate layout and write trade-offs.

questions.prompt: In the lecture’s NAND description, must reading and erasing use the same granularity?
options: Yes; both always operate on one byte
Yes; an erase block is exactly one SQL tuple
No; every read must fetch an entire erase block
No; an erase block can be larger than a read page
questions.explanation: Different granularities contribute to write trade-offs. They should not be forced into one common unit.

questions.prompt: How should the deck’s hardware prices and latency figures be used?
options: As teaching assumptions, with separate verification for real device advice
As guaranteed specifications for every current device
As proof that every I/O on every machine has equal latency
As current purchase quotations
questions.explanation: Illustrative figures are not guaranteed to be current, but they remain useful within the stated model.

questions.prompt: Which API belongs to a disk-space manager?
options: Evaluating predicates on individual records
Allocating/deallocating and reading/writing pages
Choosing join order and aggregation strategy
Tracking pin/unpin and selecting replacement victims
questions.explanation: This layer provides a page abstraction. Query semantics belong to higher layers.

questions.prompt: In an implementation using a filesystem, what can a page ID map to?
options: A position in sorted query output
An SQL alias and GROUP BY key
A filename and an offset within that file
An arbitrary tuple value without a file offset
questions.explanation: The mapping locates persistent bytes, rather than describing business data.

questions.prompt: If a needed record is on an uncached page, must the system read only that record’s exact byte count?
options: Yes; it always reads exactly one field
Yes, if the record has an id
No; it must read the entire database
No; page-granularity I/O can read the surrounding page
questions.explanation: Page granularity can bring in neighbouring bytes. It does not imply a full database scan.

questions.prompt: A file uses 4096-byte pages numbered from 0 and has no header. At what offset does page 5 begin?
questions.explanation: The offset is 5×4096. The value 24576 belongs to page 6 or reflects a numbering mistake.

questions.prompt: How does spatial control differ from temporal control?
options: Both describe only the logical order of query results
Spatial control decides where pages go; temporal control decides when to read/write them
Spatial control decides when to flush; temporal control decides storage positions
Spatial control is pin count; temporal control is record length
questions.explanation: These are the placement and timing dimensions of I/O management, not SQL clauses.
